Mollusca. Comprising soft-bodied animals such as snails, clams, squids, and octopuses, Mollusca is the second-largest phylum of invertebrates. They're characterized by several unique features, starting with the mantle—a fold of tissue that covers the animal's visceral mass and in shelled species secretes a protective shell made of calcium carbonate.

Mollusks feed using a radula, a specialized rasping ribbon of tissue lined with microscopic chitinous teeth that they use to scrape food. They also feature a muscular foot that's highly modified depending on the animal. In clams it's used for digging, in snails for crawling, and in cephalopods like squids and octopuses it forms tentacles and arms. The phylum divides into major classes. There's Gastropoda containing snails and slugs, Bivalvia containing clams and oysters and scallops, and Cephalopoda containing squids, octopuses, and cuttlefish.

Most mollusks maintain an open circulatory system where a heart pumps hemolymph into a body cavity to bathe organs directly. Cephalopods are the exception with their closed circulatory system. Mollusks share a common ciliated marine larval stage called a trochophore with annelids, even though they lack the segmented bodies that define worms. They're smaller only than arthropods, the only invertebrate phylum more diverse than Mollusca.
